passage:
Islands of Heat

A  More than two centuries ago, a London businessman in the pharmaceutical trade who had a passion for weather began keeping careful records of temperatures in the city and in the surrounding countryside. Luke Howard, who is also remembered for devising the system of cloud names still used today, noticed that the city was consistently warmer than its rural surroundings, and that the difference was greatest at night. His observations, published in the early nineteenth century, are often regarded as the first scientific description of what is now called the urban heat island.

B  The causes of the effect are now well understood. Natural landscapes are covered in vegetation and moist soil, which use much of the sun's energy to evaporate water rather than to raise temperatures. Cities replace these surfaces with asphalt, concrete and roofing materials that absorb large amounts of solar radiation and store it as heat. After sunset, this stored heat is gradually released, keeping urban air warm long into the night. Tall buildings compound the problem by trapping radiation between them and reducing the wind that might otherwise carry heat away, while vehicles, factories and air-conditioning units add waste heat of their own.

C  The size of the effect varies considerably. On a calm, clear night, the centre of a large city may be several degrees warmer than nearby farmland, whereas on a windy or cloudy day the difference may be negligible. Temperatures can also vary greatly within a single city. Neighbourhoods with many trees and parks tend to be markedly cooler than those dominated by car parks and wide roads. Studies in the United States have found that, in many cities, districts with lower average incomes have less tree cover and are consequently hotter than wealthier districts nearby.

D  These differences matter because heat is a serious threat to health. During the European heatwave of 2003, tens of thousands more people died than would normally have been expected, many of them elderly city residents living alone. High night-time temperatures are particularly dangerous, because they deprive the body of the opportunity to recover from the heat of the day. Urban heat also increases demand for air conditioning, which raises energy consumption and, in turn, releases more waste heat into the streets. In addition, higher temperatures accelerate the chemical reactions that produce ground-level ozone, a harmful air pollutant.

E  Cities have experimented with a range of responses. Painting roofs white or covering them with reflective materials can reduce the amount of solar energy absorbed; so-called green roofs, planted with vegetation, provide both shade and evaporative cooling. Some cities have trialled light-coloured coatings on roads, which can lower surface temperatures noticeably on sunny days. Planting street trees is perhaps the most widely recommended measure, since trees cool their surroundings through shade and the evaporation of water from their leaves, while also offering benefits for wildlife and mental well-being.

F  Planners are also paying more attention to the shape of cities themselves. The German city of Stuttgart, which lies in a valley prone to stagnant air, has for decades protected corridors of open land on the surrounding hillsides so that cool air can flow down into the centre at night. Such approaches require long-term planning and cooperation between departments that have traditionally worked separately. As climate change makes heatwaves more frequent and intense, the urban heat island is likely to move from being a curiosity of climate science to a central concern of urban policy.

Reconsidering the Bystander Effect

A  In March 1964, a young woman named Kitty Genovese was attacked and killed outside her apartment building in New York. Two weeks later, a newspaper report claimed that thirty-eight respectable residents had watched the attack from their windows over half an hour and that not one had called the police until it was too late. The story caused national outrage and was widely interpreted as evidence that modern city life had made people indifferent to the suffering of strangers.
